title: Order Alerts and Weekly Offers
prompt: A food delivery app sends order status alerts by push, with a text message as a fallback, and a weekly offers email. Design the notification system, using the full routine.
facts: About 8 million users; about 15 million order status alerts a day, up to 2,000 per second at dinner time; the weekly offers email goes to about 6 million users

Providers: push accepts 5,000 per second and reports within 2 minutes whether each push was delivered; SMS accepts 50 per second and costs money per message; email accepts 500 per second and an idempotency key that drops a repeated request with the same key. Push and SMS have no idempotency key
Measured: about 1% of pushes are not delivered, and about half of those users allow SMS for order alerts

Order events arrive on a queue with at-least-once delivery. The database accepts about 5,000 inserts per second under a unique key; an in-memory store runs about 100,000 "set if absent" operations per second, with a time limit per key, and acknowledges only after its replica has the change

Requirement: an order alert reaches the user's phone within 30 seconds by push; if the push is reported not delivered and the user allows SMS for order alerts, one SMS is sent instead; a user never gets the same order status twice through the same channel, and never by both push and SMS when the push was delivered

Requirement: the offers email goes only to users who are opted in at the moment of sending, never during their quiet hours (22:00 to 8:00 in their time zone), and every email is sent within 24 hours of the start
Requirement: no provider quota is ever exceeded, retries included
scope: Order alerts and the weekly offers email
Writing the message text and the offers themselves are out of scope

requirements: States push within 30 seconds with an SMS fallback only when allowed and the push was not delivered, no duplicate per channel and no push plus SMS for a delivered push, offers only to users opted in at send time and outside quiet hours within 24 hours, and quotas never exceeded
estimation: Order alerts: 2,000 per second at peak, under push's 5,000; SMS fallbacks about 2,000 × 1% × 50% = 10 per second, under 50; deduplication inserts about 2,000 per second, under 5,000
Offers: 6 million emails ÷ 500 per second = 12,000 seconds, about 3.3 hours, so quiet hours can delay some users and the batch still ends within 24 hours
design: API (notify from the order service), data model (preferences, quiet hours and time zone, a sent record per notification key), a high-level design with queues per channel and priority and a pacer per provider, and a deep dive on deduplication across retries and the fallback, and on preferences at send time
data: A notification key per order, status and user, recorded before sending, shared by the push and its SMS fallback; the email provider's key used for offers
Preferences and quiet hours read just before each send and each retry; a delay queue for users in quiet hours
tradeoffs: Names failures with conditions and a trade-off, such as: a crash between sending a push and recording it means a rare miss or a rare duplicate, and the design says which; a provider outage is retried with backoff within the quota; a summary that checks each requirement

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, deduplication in the database. Requirements: push within 30 seconds, SMS fallback only for undelivered pushes and only if allowed, no duplicate per channel, offers only to opted-in users outside quiet hours within 24 hours, quotas never exceeded. Estimates: 2,000 alerts per second at peak, about 10 SMS fallbacks per second, 2,000 key inserts per second under 5,000; offers take about 3.3 hours at 500 per second. API: notify(orderId, status, userId) from the order service. Data: preferences(user, channel, category), quiet hours and time zone; sent(key primary key, channel, status), where the key is (order, status, user). High-level: order events → workers → push queue → push pacer at 5,000 per second; a fallback check queue; SMS pacer at 50 per second; offers queue → email pacer at 500 per second, retries counted in each pacer. Deep dive: a worker inserts (order, status, user, push) before sending; a redelivered event is rejected by the unique key, so one push per status; a push found in "sending" after a crash is not resent, a rare miss. Two minutes after each push, the fallback check reads the push report; only if it was not delivered and preferences allow SMS now, it inserts (order, status, user, sms) and sends one SMS, so a delivered push never gets an SMS. Offers read preferences and the user's local time just before sending; users in quiet hours go to a delay queue until 8:00; the email key is passed to the provider, so a retry after a crash is dropped. Failures: a provider outage is retried with backoff through its pacer, so the quota holds; a worker crash before an SMS is recorded can mean a rare miss, by choice. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: the database takes every key insert.

Design B, deduplication in the in-memory store. Requirements and estimates as in Design A: 2,000 alerts per second, about 10 SMS per second, offers in about 3.3 hours. API: the same notify call. Data: preferences in the database; notification keys in the in-memory store with a 7-day time limit, acknowledged after the replica has them. High-level: the same queues and pacers; a delay queue that holds each push's fallback check for 2 minutes. Deep dive: a worker sets the key (order, status, user, push) only if absent, about 2,000 per second against 100,000, and sends only if it was new. The delayed check reads the push report after 2 minutes; if the push was not delivered and SMS is allowed at that moment, it sets the SMS key if absent and sends; otherwise nothing. Offers check preferences and quiet hours at send time and pass the key to the email provider. Failures: if the store's main copy fails, the replica, which has every acknowledged key, takes over, so no key is forgotten; pacers keep every quota, retries included. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: keys live in a store that must be run with a replica, but the database takes no extra load.

assumptions: Push reports arrive within the stated 2 minutes
reference.design:
Requirements: order alerts by push within 30 seconds; an SMS fallback only when the push was not delivered and the user allows SMS; no duplicate per channel and no SMS for a delivered push; offers only to users opted in at send time and outside 22:00 to 8:00 local time, all within 24 hours; quotas never exceeded, retries included.
Estimates: 2,000 alerts per second at peak against push's 5,000; SMS fallbacks about 2,000 × 1% × 50% = 10 per second against 50; 2,000 key inserts per second against 5,000; offers 6 million ÷ 500 = 12,000 seconds, about 3.3 hours.
API: notify(orderId, status, userId). Data: preferences, quiet hours and time zone per user; sent(key, channel, status) with (order, status, user, channel) as primary key.
Design and deep dive: workers insert the push key before sending, so a redelivered event is rejected; a push left in "sending" by a crash is not resent, accepting a rare miss. A fallback check 2 minutes later reads the push report and, only if the push was not delivered and SMS is allowed at that moment, inserts the SMS key and sends one SMS. Offers read preferences and local time just before sending, wait in a delay queue during quiet hours, and pass the key to the email provider, which drops a repeat. Each provider has a pacer that counts retries.
Failures: provider outages are retried with backoff through the pacers; a store or database problem stops new sends rather than risking duplicates. Summary: each requirement is met.
alternatives: Keys in an in-memory store with a replica and a time limit, instead of the database
Rejected: checking preferences when the offers batch is queued, because users who opt out before their email is sent would still get it
Rejected: sending the SMS at the same time as the push, because a delivered push would also get an SMS
